claim: Current technologies used to generate CRISPR/Cas gene perturbation reagents are labor intense and require multiple ligation and cloning steps.
source: Current technologies used to generate CRISPR/Cas gene perturbation reagents are labor intense and require multiple ligation and cloning steps.
evidence: This is a general statement about existing technologies presented in the abstract without specific experimental data in this manuscript, but supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Increasing gRNA sequence diversity negatively affects gRNA distribution, leading to libraries of heterogeneous quality.
source: Furthermore, increasing gRNA sequence diversity negatively affects gRNA distribution, leading to libraries of heterogeneous quality.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work in the introduction discussing PCR and cloning-dependent bias.

claim: The 3Cs technology can efficiently generate covalently-closed-circular-synthesized CRISPR/Cas gRNA reagents.
source: Here, we present a rapid and cloning-free mutagenesis technology that can efficiently generate covalently-closed-circular-synthesized (3Cs) CRISPR/Cas gRNA reagents and that uncouples sequence diversity from sequence distribution.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript showing successful generation of 3Cs gRNA libraries.

claim: The 3Cs technology uncouples sequence diversity from sequence distribution.
source: Here, we present a rapid and cloning-free mutagenesis technology that can efficiently generate covalently-closed-circular-synthesized (3Cs) CRISPR/Cas gRNA reagents and that uncouples sequence diversity from sequence distribution.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally with libraries of varying diversity (Figure 2) showing uniform distributions regardless of diversity.

claim: The fidelity and performance of 3Cs reagents was demonstrated by tailored targeting of all human deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs).
source: We demonstrate the fidelity and performance of 3Cs reagents by tailored targeting of all human deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs) and identify their essentiality for cell fitness.
evidence: This is supported by the DUB screen data presented in Figure 3 and related supplementary materials.

claim: The DUB screen identified the essentiality of DUBs for cell fitness.
source: We demonstrate the fidelity and performance of 3Cs reagents by tailored targeting of all human deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs) and identify their essentiality for cell fitness.
evidence: The manuscript presents proliferation screen data showing positive and negative fitness effects of DUB depletion.

claim: The authors generated the largest up-to-date gRNA library that can be used to interrogate the coding and noncoding human genome.
source: To explore high-content screening, we aimed to generate the largest up-to-date gRNA library that can be used to interrogate the coding and noncoding human genome and simultaneously to identify genes, predicted promoter flanking regions, transcription factors and CTCF binding sites that are linked to doxorubicin resistance.
evidence: This is supported by the description of the TGW and oTGW libraries with their diversities and target sites.

claim: The TGW library was used to identify genes, predicted promoter flanking regions, transcription factors and CTCF binding sites linked to doxorubicin resistance.
source: To explore high-content screening, we aimed to generate the largest up-to-date gRNA library that can be used to interrogate the coding and noncoding human genome and simultaneously to identify genes, predicted promoter flanking regions, transcription factors and CTCF binding sites that are linked to doxorubicin resistance.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the doxorubicin resistance screen results presented in Figure 5.

claim: CRISPR/Cas has rapidly become the gold standard for unbiased high-throughput experiments, outperforming preexisting technologies such as RNAi.
source: CRISPR/Cas has rapidly become the gold standard for unbiased high-throughput experiments, outperforming preexisting technologies such as RNAi (Evers et al., 2016; Morgens et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to comparative studies.

claim: The quality of the gRNA library, with its diversity and distribution, primarily influences downstream experimental scales.
source: A fundamentally important aspect of high-fidelity CRISPR/Cas screening is the quality of the gRNA library that is interrogated, with its diversity and distribution primarily influencing downstream experimental scales (Sanson et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work on library quality.

claim: Conventionally used methods to generate gRNA libraries include T4 ligase or homology-based cloning techniques.
source: Conventionally used methods to generate gRNA libraries in pooled or arrayed formats include T4 ligase or homology-based cloning techniques, which require the PCR-based amplification of gRNA-encoding oligonucleotides as well as the presence of open plasmid DNA for successful gRNA sequence cloning (Arakawa, 2016; Koike-Yusa et al., 2014; Ong et al., 2017; Schmidt et al., 2015; Shalem et al., 2014; Vidigal and Ventura, 2015; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established methods.

claim: Conventional library generation methods require PCR-based amplification of gRNA-encoding oligonucleotides and the presence of open plasmid DNA.
source: Conventionally used methods to generate gRNA libraries in pooled or arrayed formats include T4 ligase or homology-based cloning techniques, which require the PCR-based amplification of gRNA-encoding oligonucleotides as well as the presence of open plasmid DNA for successful gRNA sequence cloning (Arakawa, 2016; Koike-Yusa et al., 2014; Ong et al., 2017; Schmidt et al., 2015; Shalem et al., 2014; Vidigal and Ventura, 2015; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations describing conventional cloning methods.

claim: Conventional libraries contain an unwanted PCR and cloning-dependent bias in their gRNA distribution.
source: Owing to these technical constraints, conventional libraries contain an unwanted PCR and cloning-dependent bias in their gRNA distribution that influences the experimental scale required for statistically significant hit calling (Shalem et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work documenting bias in conventional libraries.

claim: The rod-shaped filamentous phage M13 differs from other bacteriophages in that its genome-packaging capacity is variable and it is present as single-stranded DNA.
source: The rod-shaped filamentous phage M13 differs from other bacteriophages in that its genome-packaging capacity is variable and in that it is present as single-stranded (ss) DNA.
evidence: This is established knowledge about M13 phage biology.

claim: Kunkel mutagenesis utilizes M13's malleable coat and the ease of ssDNA purification from M13 phage.
source: Kunkel mutagenesis utilizes M13's ﻿malleable coat and the ease of ssDNA purification from M13 phage and enables rapid site-specific mutagenesis to construct high-quality phage display libraries (Handa and Varshney, 1998; Huang et al., 2012; Kunkel, 1985; Kunkel, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational work on Kunkel mutagenesis.

claim: Kunkel mutagenesis enables rapid site-specific mutagenesis to construct high-quality phage display libraries.
source: Kunkel mutagenesis utilizes M13's ﻿malleable coat and the ease of ssDNA purification from M13 phage and enables rapid site-specific mutagenesis to construct high-quality phage display libraries (Handa and Varshney, 1998; Huang et al., 2012; Kunkel, 1985; Kunkel, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to work on phage display using Kunkel mutagenesis.

claim: Kunkel mutagenesis has significantly contributed to the great success of phage display technologies.
source: Kunkel mutagenesis has significantly contributed to the great success of phage display technologies (Ernst et al., 2013; Sidhu, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to reviews on phage display.

claim: The 3Cs technology is designed to generate CRISPR/Cas gRNA libraries robustly over a broad range of gRNA diversities.
source: In more detail, we developed a highly reproducible improved Kunkel mutagenesis technology that is designed to generate 3Cs CRISPR/Cas gRNA libraries robustly over a broad range of gRNA diversities.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the generation of libraries with diversities ranging from 256 to over 1 billion sequences.

claim: The 3Cs DUB screen confirmed previously known DUB phenotypes.
source: We demonstrate the high fidelity of 3Cs gRNA libraries by targeting all human DUBs and then determining their proliferative depletion phenotype, confirming previously known and discovering hitherto unknown DUB phenotypes.
evidence: The manuscript validates known DUB phenotypes such as USP28 and BRCC3.

claim: The 3Cs DUB screen discovered hitherto unknown DUB phenotypes.
source: We demonstrate the high fidelity of 3Cs gRNA libraries by targeting all human DUBs and then determining their proliferative depletion phenotype, confirming previously known and discovering hitherto unknown DUB phenotypes.
evidence: The manuscript identifies DUB phenotypes not previously reported in the context of proliferation.

claim: SpCas9 has nucleotide preferences including a preference for 3′ pyridine bases and disfavoring thymidine nucleotides.
source: Previously identified SpCas9 nucleotide preferences included a preference for 3′ pyridine bases whereas thymidine nucleotides are disfavored (Doench et al., 2014; Doench et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work characterizing SpCas9 preferences.

claim: The TGW oligonucleotide was designed by translating SpCas9 gRNA nucleotide preferences into a degenerated oligonucleotide sequence of 20 nucleotides.
source: In an exploratory effort, we translated SpCas9 gRNA nucleotide preferences into a degenerated oligonucleotide sequence (truly genome-wide, TGW) of 20 nucleotides, representing a theoretical diversity of 7.3 × 1010 (Figure 4A) and maximally targeting 1.65 × 107 sites in the human coding and noncoding genome (Figure 4A and Supplementary file 8).
evidence: This is described in the methods and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The TGW oligonucleotide represents a theoretical diversity of 7.3 × 10^10.
source: In an exploratory effort, we translated SpCas9 gRNA nucleotide preferences into a degenerated oligonucleotide sequence (truly genome-wide, TGW) of 20 nucleotides, representing a theoretical diversity of 7.3 × 1010 (Figure 4A) and maximally targeting 1.65 × 107 sites in the human coding and noncoding genome (Figure 4A and Supplementary file 8).
evidence: This is calculated based on the degenerate sequence design.

claim: The TGW library maximally targets 1.65 × 10^7 sites in the human coding and noncoding genome.
source: In an exploratory effort, we translated SpCas9 gRNA nucleotide preferences into a degenerated oligonucleotide sequence (truly genome-wide, TGW) of 20 nucleotides, representing a theoretical diversity of 7.3 × 1010 (Figure 4A) and maximally targeting 1.65 × 107 sites in the human coding and noncoding genome (Figure 4A and Supplementary file 8).
evidence: This is calculated based on computational analysis of the human genome.

claim: Doxorubicin-positive selection screens with the TGW library identified coding and noncoding regions linked to drug resistance.
source: Doxorubicin-positive selection screens with the TGW library in unperturbed human telomerase-immortalized retinal pigmented epithelial cells (hTERT-RPE1) were used to identify coding and noncoding regions, emphasizing the relevance of noncoding sequence elements in drug-resistance mechanisms.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the screen results presented in Figure 5.

claim: The doxorubicin screen emphasizes the relevance of noncoding sequence elements in drug-resistance mechanisms.
source: Doxorubicin-positive selection screens with the TGW library in unperturbed human telomerase-immortalized retinal pigmented epithelial cells (hTERT-RPE1) were used to identify coding and noncoding regions, emphasizing the relevance of noncoding sequence elements in drug-resistance mechanisms.
evidence: This is supported by the identification of noncoding hits including predicted promoters and CTCF binding sites.

claim: An optimized version of the TGW library (oTGW) was introduced to enable high-content functional interrogations on a truly genome-wide scale.
source: To enable high-content functional interrogations on a truly genome-wide scale, we introduce an optimized version of this library (oTGW).
evidence: The oTGW library is described and characterized in Figure 6.

claim: The 3Cs technology is established as a robust alternative method for the generation of high-quality CRISPR/Cas gene perturbation libraries.
source: In summary, we establish the 3Cs technology as a robust alternative method for the generation of high-quality CRISPR/Cas gene perturbation libraries.
evidence: This conclusion is supported by all the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Lentiviral CRISPR/Cas plasmids pLentiGuide and pLentiCRISPRv2 were successfully converted to dU-containing circular ssDNA.
source: To demonstrate its general applicability to lentiviral CRISPR/Cas plasmids, we transformed Escherichia coli CJ236 bacteria with the commonly used pLentiGuide and pLentiCRISPRv2 plasmids (Sanjana et al., 2014), both of which contain a U6 promoter-controlled non-human targeting (NHT) placeholder gRNA followed by a SpCas9 tracrRNA sequence (Doench et al., 2014; Sanjana et al., 2014).
evidence: This is demonstrated by gel electrophoresis in Figure 1B.

claim: Circular ssDNA migrated faster than dsDNA in gel electrophoresis despite being identical in length.
source: Although circular ssDNA is identical in length to dsDNA, the circular ssDNA of lentiviral CRISPR/Cas plasmids migrated faster and appeared as a single band in gel electrophoresis (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and is a known property of ssDNA.

claim: Superinfection of CJ236 culture with M13KO7 bacteriophage facilitated the generation of >30 µg of dU-containing circular ssDNA.
source: Superinfection of single-colony CJ236 culture with M13KO7 bacteriophage (108 cfu/mL) facilitated the generation of >30 µg of dU-containing circular ssDNA.
evidence: This is a reported yield from the experimental protocol.

claim: 18 nucleotides of homology (above 45°C annealing temperature) and 2 hr of 3Cs reaction time were sufficient for 3Cs reactions.
source: To gain insights into the oligonucleotide requirements and kinetics of 3Cs reactions, we tested different 3Cs homology lengths of 10, 13, 15, and 18 nucleotides, performed a 3Cs reaction time series, and demonstrated that 18 nucleotides of homology (above 45°C annealing temperature) and 2 hr of 3Cs reaction time were sufficient (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C) (Kunkel, 2001).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: 81% of pLentiGuide and 82% of plentiCRISPRv2 bacterial clones contained GFP-targeting gRNAs after 3Cs synthesis.
source: Bacterial clones were grown and their plasmid DNA Sanger sequenced, revealing that 81% of pLentiGuide and 82% of plentiCRISPRv2 contained GFP-targeting gRNAs (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is determined by Sanger sequencing of individual clones.

claim: I-SceI-mediated removal of wildtype plasmids reduced their level to below the detection limit.
source: Although the effect of increased dU concentrations was negligible, I-SceI-mediated removal of wildtype plasmids reduced their level to below our detection limit (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by NGS data showing <0.3% wildtype remnants after I-SceI digest.

claim: The plentiCRISPRv2 GFP library had an average read count of 1.15 million per GFP sequence with a wildtype rate below 0.3%.
source: We performed next-generation sequencing (NGS) on the plentiCRISPRv2 sample with an average read count of 1.15 million per GFP sequence and identified a wildtype rate of below 0.3% in the absence of any apparent sequence bias (Figure 1E and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is determined by NGS analysis.

claim: A one-sided Chi-squared test for goodness of fit identified a uniform distribution (p=0.1) of all six GFP gRNA sequences.
source: A one-sided Chi-squared test for goodness of fit identified a uniform distribution (p=0.1) of all six gRNA sequences.
evidence: This is a statistical test performed on the NGS data.

claim: The GFP library had a coefficient of variation of 33.18% and an area under the curve of 0.56.
source: The uniform gRNA distribution was supported by a low coefficient of variation (CV) of 33.18% and an area under the curve (AUC, Lorenz curve) of only 0.56 (Figure 1E–F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: These metrics are calculated from the NGS data to assess distribution uniformity.

claim: 3Cs gRNAs induced robust GFP gene editing as demonstrated by T7 Endonuclease I assay.
source: Seven days post-transduction, we performed a T7 Endonuclease I assay and observed robust GFP gene editing, both by a single GFP-targeting 3Cs gRNA (3Cs-gRNA) and by the pool of six 3Cs-gRNAs, whereas un-transduced (–) and an NHT control gRNA failed to edit the GFP gene (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the T7 endonuclease assay shown in Figure 1G.

claim: GFP gene editing by 3Cs gRNAs translated to a lentiviral dose-dependent loss of GFP protein.
source: GFP gene editing translated to a lentiviral dose-dependent loss of GFP protein when analyzed by fluorescence flow-cytometry and immunoblotting (Figure 1H–I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry and immunoblotting data in Figure 1H-I.

claim: The 3Cs technology enables the rapid and cloning-free generation of high-quality single and pooled CRISPR/Cas gRNAs.
source: Taken together, we demonstrate that the 3Cs technology enables the rapid and cloning-free generation of high-quality single and pooled CRISPR/Cas gRNAs.
evidence: This conclusion is supported by all the GFP targeting experiments.

claim: Six degenerated 3Cs oligonucleotides with increasing numbers of randomized nucleotides were designed to mimic gRNA sequence pools with diversities ranging from 256 to 262,144 individual sequences.
source: To test this hypothesis, we designed six degenerated 3Cs oligonucleotides with increasing numbers of randomized nucleotides to mimic gRNA sequence pools with diversities ranging from 256 to 262,144 individual sequences (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is described in the text and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: NGS and computational analyses identified all individual sequences in the randomized libraries with uniform distributions (AUC values between 0.6 and 0.73).
source: Independent of an oligonucleotide's diversity, NGS and computational analyses identified all of the individual sequences and uniform distributions with area under the curve values between 0.6 and 0.73 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is determined by NGS analysis and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A prominent cytosine bias was observed in the randomized libraries, with C contents above 40% within the top 10% of the most abundant gRNAs.
source: Despite the uniform distribution, we observed a prominent cytosine (C) bias in the randomized libraries, with C contents of above 40% within the top 10% of the most abundant gRNAs (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C by plotting gRNA abundance versus C content.

claim: The C bias is probably due to incomplete phosphoramidite mixing during oligonucleotide synthesis.
source: We reasoned that the C bias is probably due to incomplete phosphoramidite mixing during oligonucleotide synthesis and should therefore be absent from gRNA libraries containing nonrandom gRNA sequences (Ellington and Pollard, 2009).
evidence: This is an inference based on known issues with oligonucleotide synthesis and supported by a citation.

claim: The nonrandom DUB library was absent of C bias.
source: To test this hypothesis, we designed and generated a nonrandom 3Cs-gRNA library targeting all 105 human DUBs, each with three gRNAs (DUB library). NGS and nucleotide content analysis confirmed our hypothesis and revealed the absence of C bias from the nonrandom DUB library (Figure 2C and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by NGS analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Normalizing read counts using individual nucleotide frequencies led to improved AUC values and sequence distributions.
source: To correct the randomized libraries for the C bias, we determined the individual nucleotide frequency at every randomized position and used these frequencies to normalize the original read counts, leading to improved AUC values and sequence distributions (Figure 2D and Supplementary file 2) and further confirming the uncoupling of sequence diversity and distribution in 3Cs reactions.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the improved Lorenz curves in Figure 2D.

claim: 3Cs is a robust technology that uncouples sequence distribution from sequence diversity.
source: Taken together, these findings lead us to conclude that 3Cs is a robust technology that uncouples sequence distribution from sequence diversity and, therefore, is a powerful alternative technology to conventional gRNA cloning methods for generating gRNA libraries.
evidence: This conclusion is supported by the data from libraries with varying diversities all showing uniform distributions.

claim: The DUB proliferation screen was performed in biological duplicates with an MOI of 0.2 and library coverage of 1,000.
source: Next, we investigated the performance of 3Cs-gRNA reagents in cellular screenings. To do so, we generated infectious lentiviral particles of the 3Cs-gRNA DUB library and applied them to a proliferation screen in non-transformed hTERT–RPE1 cells in biological duplicates (multiplicity of infection (MOI) 0.2, coverage 1,000).
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the DUB screen.

claim: R2 values of 0.95, 0.88, and 0.90 were determined for time points day 0, 11, and 21, respectively, in the DUB screen.
source: In line with reports of the high experimental reproducibility of CRISPR/Cas screenings (Evers et al., 2016; Morgens et al., 2016), we determined R2 values of 0.95, 0.88, and 0.90 for time points day 0, 11, and 21, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: These correlation values are calculated from biological replicates and shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Spearman correlation and Shapiro–Wilk confidence tests revealed correlations above 0.88 and p-values below 0.001 in the DUB screen.
source: Spearman correlation and Shapiro–Wilk confidence tests revealed correlations of above 0.88 and p-values of below 0.001, respectively, demonstrating a high experimental confidence in the level of gRNA representation (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–C) (Shapiro and Wilk, 1965).
evidence: These statistical tests are performed on the replicate data.

claim: Cells depleted of USP28 or BRCC3 proliferated more rapidly than cells harboring non-human target sequences.
source: Consistent over both time points, cells depleted of USP28 or BRCC3 proliferated more rapidly than cells harboring non-human target sequences (NHTs), identifying both as negative regulators of hTERT–RPE1 proliferation (Figure 3C–D and Figure 3F and Supplementary file 4–5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the MAGeCK analysis results shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: USP28 and BRCC3 are negative regulators of hTERT–RPE1 proliferation.
source: Consistent over both time points, cells depleted of USP28 or BRCC3 proliferated more rapidly than cells harboring non-human target sequences (NHTs), identifying both as negative regulators of hTERT–RPE1 proliferation (Figure 3C–D and Figure 3F and Supplementary file 4–5).
evidence: This is inferred from the positive proliferation phenotype upon depletion.

claim: Cells depleted of PSMD14, USP7 or COPS6 proliferated less rapidly than cells harboring non-human target sequences.
source: By contrast, cells that were depleted of PSMD14, USP7 or COPS6 proliferated less rapidly than cells harboring non-human target sequences (NHTs), identifying them as positive regulators of hTERT–RPE1 proliferation (Figure 3C–D and Figure 3F and Supplementary file 4–5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the MAGeCK analysis results shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: PSMD14, USP7 and COPS6 are positive regulators of hTERT–RPE1 proliferation.
source: By contrast, cells that were depleted of PSMD14, USP7 or COPS6 proliferated less rapidly than cells harboring non-human target sequences (NHTs), identifying them as positive regulators of hTERT–RPE1 proliferation (Figure 3C–D and Figure 3F and Supplementary file 4–5).
evidence: This is inferred from the negative proliferation phenotype upon depletion.

claim: CRISPR/Cas drop out screens are performed with varying experimental durations, ranging from 5 to 15 days.
source: CRISPR/Cas drop out screens are performed with varying experimental durations, ranging from 5 to 15 days (Joung et al., 2017; Potting et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior screening studies.

claim: CRISPR/Cas induces a G1 phase arrest in p53 proficient hTERT–RPE1 cells that impacts hit calling.
source: However, recent work demonstrates that CRISPR/Cas induces a G1 phase arrest in p53 proficient hTERT–RPE1 cells that impacts hit calling (Haapaniemi et al., 2018), suggesting that later screening time points are beneficial for hit calling.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent work on p53-mediated effects.

claim: Later screening time points are beneficial for hit calling in p53 proficient cells.
source: However, recent work demonstrates that CRISPR/Cas induces a G1 phase arrest in p53 proficient hTERT–RPE1 cells that impacts hit calling (Haapaniemi et al., 2018), suggesting that later screening time points are beneficial for hit calling.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited work on p53-mediated cell cycle arrest.

claim: A trend of increased phenotype resolution among negative gene ranks over time was observed.
source: Indeed, when comparing normalized gene ranks, we observed a trend of increased phenotype resolution among negative gene ranks over time, although this effect was largely absent from positive gene ranks (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I and Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and 3).
evidence: This is observed in the data comparing day 11 and day 21 time points.

claim: The disproportional assay window of positive and negative cell proliferation phenotypes leads to higher phenotypic resolution among negative proliferative effects.
source: This effect has been reported previously and can potentially be explained by the disproportional assay window of positive and negative cell proliferation phenotypes, leading to a higher phenotypic resolution among negative proliferative effects (Shalem et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This explanation is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Depletion of USP28 and USP46 induced the strongest positive change in phenotype between day 11 and day 21.
source: Depletion of USP28 and USP46 induced the strongest positive change, whereas deletion of USP22, USP48 or TNFAIP3 induced the most significant negative change, in phenotype between day 11 and day 21, suggesting a time-dependent absence of compensatory mechanisms to accommodate an early loss-of-function phenotype (Figure 3E–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 3I).
evidence: This is shown in the time-dependent analysis in Figure 3E-F.

claim: Deletion of USP22, USP48 or TNFAIP3 induced the most significant negative change in phenotype between day 11 and day 21.
source: Depletion of USP28 and USP46 induced the strongest positive change, whereas deletion of USP22, USP48 or TNFAIP3 induced the most significant negative change, in phenotype between day 11 and day 21, suggesting a time-dependent absence of compensatory mechanisms to accommodate an early loss-of-function phenotype (Figure 3E–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 3I).
evidence: This is shown in the time-dependent analysis in Figure 3E-F.

claim: Time-dependent phenotype changes suggest a time-dependent absence of compensatory mechanisms to accommodate an early loss-of-function phenotype.
source: Depletion of USP28 and USP46 induced the strongest positive change, whereas deletion of USP22, USP48 or TNFAIP3 induced the most significant negative change, in phenotype between day 11 and day 21, suggesting a time-dependent absence of compensatory mechanisms to accommodate an early loss-of-function phenotype (Figure 3E–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 3I).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the time-dependent phenotype data.

claim: Depletion of USP28 and BRCC3 induced a rapid positive proliferation effect as validated by shRNA.
source: When compared to negative- (Luciferase) and positive-control (Plk1) shRNA sequences, depletion of USP28 and BRCC3 induced a rapid positive proliferation effect (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the validation experiment shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Depletion of USP7 and COPS6 induced an instant and strong negative proliferation effect as validated by shRNA.
source: By contrast, depletion of USP7 and COPS6 induced an instant and strong negative proliferation effect (Figure 3G), validating the gRNA-mediated knockout phenotypes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the validation experiment shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The shRNA validation experiments validate the gRNA-mediated knockout phenotypes.
source: By contrast, depletion of USP7 and COPS6 induced an instant and strong negative proliferation effect (Figure 3G), validating the gRNA-mediated knockout phenotypes.
evidence: The shRNA results are consistent with the gRNA screen results.

claim: The analysis demonstrates the quality and fidelity of 3Cs reagents in functional genomics applications.
source: Collectively, our analysis demonstrates the quality and fidelity of 3Cs reagents in functional genomics applications.
evidence: This conclusion is supported by the DUB screen and validation data.

claim: CRISPR/Cas technology has become the method of choice for gene perturbation experiments.
source: Owing to its versatility,CRISPR/Cas technology has become the method of choice for gene perturbation experiments, yet classical short hairpin RNAs (shRNA, RNAi) are still widely used.
evidence: This is a general statement about the field supported by common knowledge.

claim: Classical short hairpin RNAs (shRNA, RNAi) are still widely used.
source: Owing to its versatility,CRISPR/Cas technology has become the method of choice for gene perturbation experiments, yet classical short hairpin RNAs (shRNA, RNAi) are still widely used.
evidence: This is a general statement about the field supported by common knowledge.

claim: shRNA oligonucleotides contain complementary sequences that form stable secondary structures that render the generation of shRNA reagents inefficient.
source: However, shRNA oligonucleotides contain complementary sequences that form stable secondary structures that render the generation of shRNA reagents inefficient (McIntyre and Fanning, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work on shRNA synthesis challenges.

claim: The denaturation and annealing step in 3Cs circumvents the secondary structures of shRNA oligonucleotides.
source: A crucial step in our improved Kunkel mutagenesis technology is the denaturation of the gRNA-encoding oligonucleotides and their subsequent annealing to template ssDNA (see 'Materials and methods' section). Owing to this denaturation and annealing step, we anticipated that improved Kunkel mutagenesis would circumvent the secondary structures of shRNA oligonucleotide and enable the generation of shRNA reagents.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the protocol design.

claim: 3Cs reactions using 60 ng and 120 ng of ssDNA yielded the characteristic 3Cs-DNA band pattern with no major difference in bacterial transformation efficiency.
source: We performed two parallel 3Cs reactions using 60 ng and 120 ng of ssDNA, and both reactions yielded the characteristic 3Cs-DNA band pattern with no major difference in bacterial transformation efficiency between the two tested scales (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by gel electrophoresis in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: SANGER sequencing confirmed the successful integration of the GFP–shRNA sequence into pLKO.1.
source: To demonstrate the successful integration of the GFP–shRNA sequence into pLKO.1, we amplified single bacterial clones carrying 3Cs-DNA of shRNA reactions and analyzed their plasmid DNA by SANGER sequencing. This resulted in the expected GFP–shRNA sequence and the absence of adjacent nucleotide changes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D), from which we concluded that 3Cs is a versatile technology that generates high-quality gRNA and shRNA reagents.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Sanger sequencing shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claim: 3Cs is a versatile technology that generates high-quality gRNA and shRNA reagents.
source: To demonstrate the successful integration of the GFP–shRNA sequence into pLKO.1, we amplified single bacterial clones carrying 3Cs-DNA of shRNA reactions and analyzed their plasmid DNA by SANGER sequencing. This resulted in the expected GFP–shRNA sequence and the absence of adjacent nucleotide changes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D), from which we concluded that 3Cs is a versatile technology that generates high-quality gRNA and shRNA reagents.
evidence: This conclusion is supported by successful generation of both gRNA and shRNA reagents.

claim: GFP-targeting 3Cs-shRNA reduced GFP-fluorescence by more than 60% in transduced cells.
source: To demonstrate 3Cs-shRNA fidelity, we generated infectious lentiviral particles of the GFP-targeting 3Cs-shRNA and transduced GFP-positive hTERT–RPE1 cells. Strikingly, 96 hr after lentiviral transduction, we observed a reduction in GFP-fluorescence, confirming the functionality of the 3Cs-shRNAs in cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E.

claim: The E2 3Cs-shRNA library had a wildtype remnant level of 0.04%, a CV of 37.9% and an AUC of 0.68.
source: To determine the E2 3Cs-shRNA distribution more accurately, we performed NGS sequencing with an average shRNA read count of >8,300 and determined a wildtype remnant level of 0.04%, a CV of 37.9% and an AUC of 0.68, demonstrating an almost uniform distribution (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D–E).
evidence: These metrics are calculated from NGS data.

claim: The Bsu36I digest does not affect 3Cs-shRNA sequence distribution.
source: To correlate 3Cs-shRNA abundance and the distribution of the E2 3Cs-shRNA libraries before and after Bsu36I enzyme digest, we determined the ratios of their respective normalized read counts. Importantly, all ratios were close to one and lined up close to the respective diagonal with a linear regression R2 of 0.9687 (Figure 3—figure supplement 5F), demonstrating a high correlation of individual data points and no influence of the Bsu36I digest on 3Cs-shRNA sequence distribution.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing distributions before and after digest in Figure 3—figure supplement 5F.

claim: The 3Cs technology can be adapted to generate high-quality shRNA reagents in single and pooled formats.
source: In summary, this demonstrates that our 3Cs technology can be adapted to generate high-quality shRNA reagents in single and pooled formats.
evidence: This conclusion is supported by the successful generation of single and pooled shRNA libraries.

claim: 3Cs gRNA library diversity is mostly limited by the number of distinguishable oligonucleotides within a 3Cs reaction and the subsequent bacterial electroporation efficiencies.
source: Thus, we hypothesized that 3Cs gRNA library diversity is mostly limited by the number of distinguishable oligonucleotides within a 3Cs reaction and the subsequent bacterial electroporation efficiencies.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the technical aspects of the method.

claim: Limitations in electroporation efficiencies can be overcome by accumulating the individual efficiencies of multiple parallel reactions.
source: Limitations in electroporation efficiencies can be overcome by accumulating the individual efficiencies of multiple parallel reactions, as routinely performed to amplify phage libraries with diversities beyond 109 (Smith and Scott, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work on phage library amplification.

claim: The number of distinguishable oligonucleotides is limited by the capacity of synthetic oligonucleotide synthesis.
source: The number of distinguishable oligonucleotides is limited by the capacity of synthetic oligonucleotide synthesis, rendering truly genome-wide gene perturbation libraries unfeasible.
evidence: This is a statement about the technical limitations of oligonucleotide synthesis.

claim: A cumulative transformation efficiency of 1.2 × 10^10 was achieved for the TGW library, accounting for ~16% of TGW sequences.
source: Importantly, we note that the amplification of this degenerated library is limited by the number of transformed bacteria. As complete generation of this reagent is currently unfeasible, we limited our efforts to eight parallel electroporation reactions and achieved a cumulative transformation efficiency of 1.2 × 1010, accounting for ~16% of TGW sequences, assuming a stringent uniform sequence distribution.
evidence: This is a measured transformation efficiency from the experimental protocol.

claim: 94.19% of TGW NGS reads were unique.
source: In order to approximate the gRNA distribution, we generated 14.4 million NGS reads and found 94.19% to be unique (Figure 4C and Supplementary file 9).
evidence: This is determined by NGS analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The nucleotide frequencies extracted from TGW NGS reads matched the initially applied degenerated oligonucleotide sequence.
source: We went on to extract the nucleotide frequencies for each gRNA position from TGW NGS reads, translated them to IUPAC nomenclature, and identified the identical degenerated sequence that we initially applied in the form of the degenerated oligonucleotide pool (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the nucleotide frequency analysis in Figure 4D.

claim: The TGW library had a CV of 0.26% and an AUC of 0.52, suggesting a nearly uniform distribution.
source: Furthermore, the distribution of TGW read counts had a CV of 0.26% and an AUC of 0.52, suggesting a nearly uniform distribution of sequenced and represented gRNA sequences (Figure 4E–F) (Makowski and Soares, 2003).
evidence: These metrics are calculated from NGS data and shown in Figure 4E-F.

claim: Doxorubicin induces a robust, irreversible and dose-dependent reduction of cell viability in hTERT–RPE1 cells within 4 days.
source: In hTERT–RPE1 cells, doxorubicin induces a robust, irreversible and dose-dependent reduction of cell viability within 4 days (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the dose-response curve in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 5.5 × 10^8 infectious lentiviral particles of the TGW library were generated for the doxorubicin resistance screen.
source: We therefore generated 5.5 × 108 infectious lentiviral particles of the TGW library and applied them to screen for resistance to doxorubicin (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This is the reported titer of lentivirus used in the screen.

claim: The experimental reproducibility of the TGW doxorubicin screen was low (0.004%).
source: Although the experimental reproducibility was low (0.004%), we identified an experimental overlap of 4,232 gRNAs, with associated Spearman ranking and Pearson correlations of above 0.75 (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is calculated from the overlap of hits across three replicates.

claim: An experimental overlap of 4,232 gRNAs was identified across three TGW screen replicates.
source: Although the experimental reproducibility was low (0.004%), we identified an experimental overlap of 4,232 gRNAs, with associated Spearman ranking and Pearson correlations of above 0.75 (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in the Venn diagram in Figure 5C.

claim: The validation screen reidentified 2,716 gRNAs of which 795 were more than two-fold enriched after 21 d of doxorubicin treatment.
source: As a result, we reidentified 2,716 gRNAs of which 795 were more than two-fold enriched after 21 d of doxorubicin treatment when compared to the untreated control (Figure 5D and Supplementary file 11).
evidence: This is shown in the validation screen results in Figure 5D.

claim: Seven gRNAs were identified to target five genes (PDE8B, AVPR2, CYSLTR2, IL3RA, and POLE2).
source: We identified seven gRNAs to target five genes (PDE8B, AVPR2, CYSLTR2, IL3RA, and POLE2), of which PDE8B and AVPR2 were targeted by two gRNAs, and a single gRNA sequence matched a noncoding location within chromosome 8 (chr8:93022800) (Figure 5E and Figure 5G and Supplementary file 12–13).
evidence: This is determined by mapping gRNA sequences to the genome using Cas-OFFinder.

claim: CysLTR2 is a Leukotriene C4 G-protein-coupled eicosanoid receptor that was recently reported to induce doxorubicin resistance by abolishing the accumulation of reactive oxygen species.
source: The coding hits that we identified included CysLTR2, a Leukotriene C4 G-protein-coupled eicosanoid receptor that was recently reported to induce doxorubicin resistance by abolishing the accumulation of reactive oxygen species (Dvash et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work on CysLTR2.

claim: Chemical inhibition of CysLTR2 with Bay-CysLT2 or Bay-u9773 reverted doxorubicin-induced toxicity in a dose-dependent manner.
source: To validate CysLTR2 as a doxorubicin-resistance inducing hit, we chemically inhibited CysLTR2 with increasing concentrations of Bay-CysLT2 or Bay-u9773 in the presence of doxorubicin and quantified cell viability by AlamarBlue staining. Importantly, both drugs reverted the doxorubicin-induced toxicity in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 5F), suggesting that the loss of CysLTR2 causes doxorubicin resistance.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the chemical inhibition experiment in Figure 5F.

claim: The loss of CysLTR2 causes doxorubicin resistance.
source: To validate CysLTR2 as a doxorubicin-resistance inducing hit, we chemically inhibited CysLTR2 with increasing concentrations of Bay-CysLT2 or Bay-u9773 in the presence of doxorubicin and quantified cell viability by AlamarBlue staining. Importantly, both drugs reverted the doxorubicin-induced toxicity in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 5F), suggesting that the loss of CysLTR2 causes doxorubicin resistance.
evidence: This is inferred from the chemical inhibition experiment showing that blocking CysLTR2 reverses resistance.

claim: 192 gRNAs (22.38% of 795 gRNAs) could be mapped to coding regions when allowing up to two mismatches.
source: As expected, the number of gRNAs that could be mapped to the reference genome increased to 192 and 222 for coding and noncoding target sites, respectively, accounting for 50.3% of the 795 gRNAs (Figure 5E and Supplementary file 12).
evidence: This is shown in the pie chart in Figure 5E.

claim: 222 gRNAs (27.92% of 795 gRNAs) could be mapped to noncoding regions when allowing up to two mismatches.
source: As expected, the number of gRNAs that could be mapped to the reference genome increased to 192 and 222 for coding and noncoding target sites, respectively, accounting for 50.3% of the 795 gRNAs (Figure 5E and Supplementary file 12).
evidence: This is shown in the pie chart in Figure 5G.

claim: Three gRNAs targeted two different coding positions within the AKAP6 gene.
source: Interestingly, when mismatches are allowed, we identified three gRNAs that targeted two different coding positions within the AKAP6 gene (chr14:32671632, chr14:32784395), as well as five different gRNAs that targeted the exact same coding position within the ASPA2 gene (chr2:9229295) (Figure 5E and Supplementary file 12).
evidence: This is determined by genome mapping analysis.

claim: Five different gRNAs targeted the exact same coding position within the ASPA2 gene.
source: Interestingly, when mismatches are allowed, we identified three gRNAs that targeted two different coding positions within the AKAP6 gene (chr14:32671632, chr14:32784395), as well as five different gRNAs that targeted the exact same coding position within the ASPA2 gene (chr2:9229295) (Figure 5E and Supplementary file 12).
evidence: This is determined by genome mapping analysis.

claim: Four gRNAs targeted four different positions on chromosome X in close proximity to the SPIN2A gene.
source: Within the noncoding gRNA target sites, we identified four gRNAs that targeted four different positions on chromosome X (56546543, 57766898, 63133046, 63245878), all of which are in close proximity to the SPIN2A gene (Figure 5G and Supplementary file 13), suggesting a doxorubicin-tolerance-inducing function in this locus.
evidence: This is determined by genome mapping analysis.

claim: The SPIN2A locus has a doxorubicin-tolerance-inducing function.
source: Within the noncoding gRNA target sites, we identified four gRNAs that targeted four different positions on chromosome X (56546543, 57766898, 63133046, 63245878), all of which are in close proximity to the SPIN2A gene (Figure 5G and Supplementary file 13), suggesting a doxorubicin-tolerance-inducing function in this locus.
evidence: This is inferred from the clustering of hits near SPIN2A.

claim: 25 genes match the UV_RESPONSE_VIA_ERCC3 group (downregulated in mutant ERCC3-expressing fibroblasts) as the most significant hit in molecular signature analysis.
source: In order to reveal whether the identified set of coding genes correlated with reported phenotypes or gene ontologies, we performed a molecular signature analysis of the 178 coding target regions and identified 25 genes that match the UV_RESPONSE_VIA_ERCC3 (downregulated in mutant ERCC3-expressing fibroblasts) group as the most significant hit (p-value of 6.11E-17) (Figure 5H–I and Supplementary file 14).
evidence: This is determined by molecular signature database analysis shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Doxorubicin-induced interstrand crosslinks are repaired by ERCC3-dependent nucleotide excision repair (NER).
source: Importantly, doxorubicin-induced interstrand crosslinks are repaired by ERCC3-dependent nucleotide excision repair (NER), and NER-deficient cells have been shown to display greater tolerance to adduct-forming anthracycline treatment, connecting these 25 genes to an increased doxorubicin tolerance (Bret et al., 2013; Spencer et al., 2008; van Brabant et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on DNA repair mechanisms.

claim: NER-deficient cells display greater tolerance to adduct-forming anthracycline treatment.
source: Importantly, doxorubicin-induced interstrand crosslinks are repaired by ERCC3-dependent nucleotide excision repair (NER), and NER-deficient cells have been shown to display greater tolerance to adduct-forming anthracycline treatment, connecting these 25 genes to an increased doxorubicin tolerance (Bret et al., 2013; Spencer et al., 2008; van Brabant et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Mutations in noncoding sequences have been linked to the misregulation of adjacently located genes by disrupting cis-regulatory elements.
source: Furthermore, mutations in noncoding sequences have been linked to the misregulation of adjacently located genes by disrupting cis-regulatory elements (Hnisz et al., 2016; Katainen et al., 2015; Weinhold et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on noncoding mutations.

claim: Noncoding target sites include predicted promoters (12.6%), lincRNAs (11.3%), processed pseudogenes (4.5%) and CTCF binding sites (3.6%).
source: Therefore, we searched for available biotypes that are associated with the identified noncoding target regions and were able to identify target sites matching 'predicted promoter' (12.6%), 'lincRNAs' (11.3%) as well as 'processed pseudogenes' (4.5%) and 'CTCF binding sites' (3.6%) annotations (Figure 5J and Supplementary file 13).
evidence: This is shown in the pie chart in Figure 5J.

claim: 52.7% of noncoding gRNAs have no available biotype or genomic annotation.
source: However, no biotype or genomic annotation was available for 52.7% of the noncoding gRNAs, and we therefore identified the nearest 5′ and 3′ located genes and used them to perform a molecular signature analysis (Figure 5K and Supplementary file 15).
evidence: This is shown in the pie chart in Figure 5J.

claim: Genes regulated by transcription factors FOXO4, KLF1, and NFAT were enriched among the four most enriched molecular signatures for noncoding hits.
source: Among the four most enriched molecular signatures, we identified genes that are regulated by the transcription factors FOXO4, KLF1, and NFAT, noting that FOXO4 and NFAT downregulation has previously been reported to increase doxorubicin tolerance (Figure 5K and Supplementary file 15).
evidence: This is shown in the molecular signature analysis in Figure 5K.

claim: FOXO4 and NFAT downregulation has previously been reported to increase doxorubicin tolerance.
source: Among the four most enriched molecular signatures, we identified genes that are regulated by the transcription factors FOXO4, KLF1, and NFAT, noting that FOXO4 and NFAT downregulation has previously been reported to increase doxorubicin tolerance (Figure 5K and Supplementary file 15).
evidence: This is stated as prior knowledge but not directly cited in this sentence.

claim: gRNAs truncated to 17 nt maintain on-target efficiencies while reducing off-target effects.
source: In line with this, gRNAs that are truncated to 17 nt have been demonstrated to maintain on-target efficiencies while reducing off-target effects (Fu et al., 2014; Wyvekens et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on truncated gRNAs.

claim: The oTGW oligonucleotide has a total diversity of 1.5 × 10^9.
source: We therefore truncated the degenerated TGW oligonucleotide sequence to 17 nt(optimized TGA, oTGW), approximating to a a total oligonucleotide diversity of 1.5 × 109 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is calculated based on the truncated degenerate sequence.

claim: The oTGW sequence diversity is 50-times smaller than the TGW sequence diversity.
source: Importantly, the oTGW sequence diversity is 50-times smaller than the TGW sequence diversity, while the 1.65 × 107 unique target sequences in the human genome remain identical (Figure 6A and Supplementary file 8).
evidence: This is calculated by comparing the diversities of TGW and oTGW.

claim: The 1.65 × 10^7 unique target sequences in the human genome remain identical between TGW and oTGW.
source: Importantly, the oTGW sequence diversity is 50-times smaller than the TGW sequence diversity, while the 1.65 × 107 unique target sequences in the human genome remain identical (Figure 6A and Supplementary file 8).
evidence: This is determined by computational analysis of genome target sites.

claim: The three oTGW libraries had an average wildtype remnant rate of 0.2%.
source: Furthermore, an average wildtype remnant rate of 0.2% was determined and AUC values were 0.54 or below (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting a uniform distribution of represented gRNA sequences in all three oTGW libraries (Makowski and Soares, 2003).
evidence: This is determined by NGS analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The three oTGW libraries had AUC values of 0.54 or below.
source: Furthermore, an average wildtype remnant rate of 0.2% was determined and AUC values were 0.54 or below (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting a uniform distribution of represented gRNA sequences in all three oTGW libraries (Makowski and Soares, 2003).
evidence: This is calculated from NGS data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The oTGW libraries are the first of their kind and have the potential to elevate functional genomics approaches.
source: Thus, these oTGW libraries are the first of their kind, have the potential to elevate functional genomics approaches and will be made available to the scientific community by the Goethe University Depository (http://www.innovectis.de/INNOVECTIS-Frankfurt/Technologieangebote/Depository).
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty and potential impact of the libraries.

claim: The 3Cs technology has several unique features including applicability to all plasmids containing a f1-origin of replication.
source: The 3Cs technology has several unique features. First, the bacteriophage-mediated generation of ssDNA makes the technology applicable to all plasmids containing a f1-origin of replication.
evidence: This is a statement about the general applicability of the method.

claim: ssDNA-mutagenic oligonucleotides are annealed to the ssDNA of the template DNA, thereby circumventing the need for two oligonucleotides per gRNA and amplification by PCR.
source: Second, ssDNA-mutagenic oligonucleotides are annealed to the ssDNA of the template DNA, thereby circumventing the need for two oligonucleotides per gRNA and amplification by PCR, reducing associated costs and sequence bias.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the 3Cs method compared to conventional approaches.

claim: T7 DNA polymerase has an error rate of approximately 15 × 10^-6.
source: In line with this, T7 DNA polymerase, which is used in the 3Cs reaction, has an error rate of approximately 15 × 10−6, resulting in as little as 0.0015% of mutated heteroduplex 3Cs product assuming 2 µg ssDNA of a 10 kb plasmid (Kong et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work on T7 polymerase fidelity.

claim: The presence of a gRNA placeholder sequence enables the near-complete removal of wildtype plasmid remnants.
source: Third, the presence of a gRNA placeholder sequence enables the near-complete removal of wildtype plasmid remnants.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the I-SceI digest experiments throughout the manuscript.

claim: The plasmid range of 3Cs can be expanded to recombinant Adeno-Associated Virus (rAAV) plasmids and adenoviruses.
source: Last, we demonstrate 3Cs applicability and performance using the example of lentiviral plasmids. However, we foresee the plasmid range to be expanded to recombinant Adeno-Associated Virus (rAAV) plasmids and adenoviruses, as well as coding sequences for protein mutagenesis that enable in-cell and in-vivo functional screenings.
evidence: This is a speculation about future applications of the technology.

claim: Depletion of USP28 was recently identified as preventing p53 elevation in response to centrosome loss resulting from Plk4 inhibition.
source: In line with this, USP28 was recently identified as preventing p53 elevation in response to centrosome loss resulting from Plk4 inhibition, thereby preventing growth arrest in response to prolonged mitosis (Meitinger et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work on USP28.

claim: COPS6 and USP7 have been implicated in DNA damage response and enhanced p53 stability, leading to a prolonged G1-phase cell cycle arrest.
source: Among them are COPS6 and USP7, both of which have been implicated in DNA damage response and enhanced p53 stability, leading to a prolonged G1-phase cell cycle arrest (Li et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: DNA damage-associated DUBs (e.g. COPS6 or USP7) can be used as p53 alternatives to control for DNA-damage-induced cell cycle arrest in CRISPR/Cas functional genomic screens.
source: In line with this, recent work demonstrates a direct connection between CRISPR/Cas gene editing and a p53-dependent DNA damage response that is associated with G1 cell cycle arrest (Haapaniemi et al., 2018), suggesting that DNA damage-associated DUBs (e.g. COPS6 or USP7) can be used as p53 alternatives to control for DNA-damage-induced cell cycle arrest and negative hit calling in CRISPR/Cas functional genomic screens.
evidence: This is a suggestion based on the integration of the DUB screen results with prior knowledge about p53 and CRISPR effects.

claim: A fully randomized library with oligonucleotides of length 20 comprises 4^20 = 1.1*10^12 different sequences.
source: A fully randomized library with oligonucleotides of length 20 (20N) resembles the entire space of possible gRNA sequences and comprises 420 = 1.1*1012 different sequences.
evidence: This is a mathematical calculation.

claim: The ~300 million SpCas9 target sites in the human genome would represent only 0.027% of a fully randomized 20N library.
source: The ~300 million SpCas9 target sites in the human genome would be covered by a fully randomized library, but would represent only 0.027% of the library.
evidence: This is calculated based on the number of target sites and library diversity.

claim: Screening the 20N library with a coverage of 100 and a MOI of 0.5 would require 2.2*10^14 cells.
source: Screening the 20N library with a coverage of 100 and a MOI of 0.5 would require 2.2*1014 cells, a cell number that is clearly not feasible in current experimental setups.
evidence: This is calculated based on library diversity and desired coverage.

claim: The computational approach for coding and noncoding hit-calling is sensitive to incorrect calling of cut sites that can lead to false-positive target regions.
source: Furthermore, our computational approach for coding and noncoding hit-calling is sensitive to incorrect calling of cut sites that can lead to false-positive target regions.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: Using the actual genome sequence of the cell line of interest is suggested to limit false-positive hit calling.
source: We therefore suggest that the actual genome sequence of the cell line of interest is used in order to limit false-positive hit calling.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the limitations of using the reference genome.

claim: The human reference genome (GRCh38.86) might differ from the hTERT–RPE1 genome, potentially giving misleading conclusions in terms of hit calling.
source: We used the human reference genome (GRCh38.86), which might differ from the hTERT–RPE1 genome, potentially giving misleading conclusions in terms of hit calling.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: The oTGW CRISPR/Cas gRNA libraries are suitable for broad biological screenings with the highest genetic target complexity.
source: We propose that the oTGW CRISPR/Cas gRNA libraries are suitable for broad biological screenings with the highest genetic target complexity.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the characteristics of the oTGW libraries.

claim: oTGW screens can be followed by targeted validation screens using newly synthesized libraries tailored to initially identified cut sites.
source: Such screens can be followed by targeted validation screens using newly synthesized libraries that are tailored to the initially identified cut sites, which will enable rapid functional validation of such complex genetic experiments.
evidence: This is a suggested workflow for using the oTGW libraries.
